claim: An intermediary market of self-styled algorithmic experts sells optimisation advice, analytics and services to creators for fees and percentages, imposing an unmeasured drag on net creator income that gross-earnings statistics ignore.
stance_target: The claim that gross creator earnings systematically overstate net creator income because of unrecorded costs paid to intermediaries
scope_conditions: YouTube, UK/US ecosystem, three years of ethnographic fieldwork published 2020; qualitative, no sample size given for the expert population and no cost figures quantified; WESTERN-ONLY
quoted_support: advertising, brand deals, and analytics in return for a percent-

claim: Algorithmic-expert discourse frames platform visibility as meritocratic and offers only individualised solutions, so creators who fail are supplied with an explanatory frame that attributes failure to their own insufficient optimisation rather than to structural distribution.
stance_target: The reliability of creator self-reported quit reasons, which are shaped by an industry discourse that systematically relocates causation from platform structure to individual effort
scope_conditions: YouTube, UK/US, ethnographic study published 2020; interpretive claim from qualitative fieldwork, not a measured effect on reported quit reasons; WESTERN-ONLY
quoted_support: their meritocratic framing offers only individualized solutions that ignore systemic inequalities on social media platforms

claim: Creators lack visibility into their own audience composition, as illustrated by a creator discovering her audience was 90% men despite content aimed elsewhere -- so creator-reported explanations of performance are built on incomplete information.
stance_target: The claim that creators cannot accurately diagnose why their content does or does not monetise, which undermines the evidentiary value of self-reported quit reasons
scope_conditions: YouTube, single case within a qualitative ethnography; WESTERN-ONLY
